newsitem.title: USA: U.S. officials try to dispel rumors in TWA crash.
newsitem.headline: U.S. officials try to dispel rumors in TWA crash.

text.p: Two months into the investigation of the TWA Flight 800 crash, exasperated officials on Monday sought to dispel persistent rumors that "friendly-fire" brought down the plane over the Atlantic killing all 230 people on board.

Lead investigators told their first news conference since Sept. 5 that none of the three theories on the cause of the aircraft explosion on July 17 had been ruled out. These included a bomb, a missile or catastrophic mechanical failure.

"We've looked at every aspect of what could have caused this tragedy," said New York FBI head James Kallstrom. "I've said publicly many, many times that friendly fire is highly, highly, highly, highly unlikely. The notion that this did happen ... and that all the people working here are covering this up is an outrageous accusation."

In the absence of definitive evidence on the cause of the crash -- apart from microscopic traces of chemical explosive on some aircraft wreckage -- there has been speculation in the media and among the public that so-called friendly fire from U.S. military forces accidentally brought down the Boeing 747 and that the U.S. government was covering it up.

The aircraft exploded in mid-air without warning just 11-1/2 minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy airport on a flight to Paris and its wreckage was strewn over a wide area off the small town of East Moriches on New York's Long Island. The bodies or remains of 213 victims have been recovered.

National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) vice chairman Robert Francis told reporters that investigators were considering a number of options in which to use another Boeing 747 in the probe but had not decided to simulate an explosion. He also said that investigators would only consider dredging the ocean floor if they believed there was material valuable to the probe.

"We understand very well the sense of urgency in terms of finding out what's happening but we also understand that it is even more important that this be done accurately and responsibly," said Francis. "We have no great interest in this going on and on."

The NTSB official said U.S. Navy divers would continue to search the ocean for wreckage, which was being brought to land and sent to an aircraft hangar at Calverton, Long Island for analysis and reconstruction.
